chunks.title: Conjunctiva anatomy in 1 minute
chunks.tldr: Three parts: palpebral (stuck to the tarsus), forniceal (loose), bulbar (on the eye). Limbal stem cells live in the palisades of Vogt.
points: Lymph drains to the preauricular and submandibular nodes (same as the lids).
Bulbar conjunctiva fuses with Tenon at the limbus. Palisades of Vogt = corneal stem cell reservoir.
Epithelium: non-keratinised, ~5 cells thick. Goblet cells are densest inferonasally and in the fornices.
Stroma holds the accessory lacrimal glands (Krause, Wolfring) and immune tissue (CALT).
Medially: plica semilunaris + caruncle (modified skin).
chunks.hook: Vogt = the vault where stem cells are stored.

cards.q: Where are the corneal limbal stem cells thought to reside?

chunks.title: Reading a red eye: discharge & reactions
chunks.tldr: Itch = allergy. Watery = viral/allergic. Pus = bacterial. Lots of pus = gonococcus. Real pain/photophobia = the cornea is involved.
points: Discharge: watery (viral, acute allergy) → mucoid (chronic allergy, dry eye) → mucopurulent (chlamydia, bacteria) → hyperpurulent (gonococcus).
Conjunctival injection = beefy red, worse away from the limbus. Ciliary flush (uveitis) = worst at the limbus.
Petechial haemorrhages → viral. Big haemorrhages → severe bacterial.
Chemosis: acute = allergy. Chronic = TED, SVC obstruction, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome.
Pseudomembrane peels off cleanly. True membrane tears and bleeds. Causes: adenovirus, gonococcus, Strep, diphtheria, ligneous, SJS.
Lymph nodes (preauricular): viral, chlamydia, gonococcus, Parinaud.
chunks.hook: Discharge ladder: Water → Mucus → Pus → Flood of pus (gonococcus).

cards.q: Hyperacute profuse purulent discharge suggests?
Membrane that bleeds when peeled: true or pseudo?

chunks.title: Follicles vs papillae
chunks.tldr: Follicles = rice grains with vessels around them (lymphoid). Papillae = red dots with a vessel in the middle.
points: Follicles: pale, translucent, mainly in the fornices. Histology: lymphoid germinal centre.
Follicle causes: viral, chlamydia, Parinaud, drug hypersensitivity (e.g. brimonidine, atropine). Small follicles are normal in kids.
Papillae: only where the conjunctiva is tethered (tarsus, limbus). Central vascular core.
Sizes: micro → macro (<1 mm) → giant (>1 mm).
Papillae causes: bacterial, allergy, blepharitis, contact lenses, SLK, floppy eyelid.
chunks.hook: Follicle = Forniceal, viral. Papilla = has a Pipe (vessel) in the middle.

cards.q: Which has a central vascular core: follicle or papilla?

chunks.title: Acute bacterial conjunctivitis
chunks.tldr: Sticky, red, lids glued shut in the morning. 60% settle in 5 days anyway. Gonococcus/meningococcus need systemic antibiotics.
points: Common bugs: Strep pneumoniae, Staph aureus, H. influenzae, Moraxella.
Gonococcus can get through intact cornea → ulcer → perforation. Gram stain: Gram-negative kidney-shaped intracellular diplococci. Culture on chocolate / Thayer–Martin agar.
Usually both eyes (one first), mucopurulent, vision normal, no nodes (unless gonococcal).
Treat: topical antibiotic QID for a week (none is better than another). No contact lenses until 48 h after it clears.
Gonococcus → IM/IV ceftriaxone + hourly topical + GUM referral.
H. influenzae in kids → oral co-amoxiclav (25% get otitis).
Meningococcus in kids → systemic antibiotics now (30% go systemic).
Giant fornix syndrome: elderly person with levator disinsertion, debris in a huge upper fornix → recurrent Staph pus. Sweep the fornix + antibiotics.
chunks.hook: Gono goes through (intact cornea). Treat the body, not just the eye.

chunks.title: Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis
chunks.tldr: Young sexually active adult, months of follicular conjunctivitis + tender preauricular node. Serovars D–K. Treat with oral azithromycin + GUM referral.
points: Chlamydia trachomatis D–K. Spread from genital secretions to the eye. Incubation ~1 week.
Men: often silent urethritis. Women: PID → infertility, Fitz-Hugh–Curtis (perihepatitis). Can trigger reactive arthritis.
Eye: large follicles in the inferior fornix (and upper tarsus), tender preauricular nodes, SPK, peripheral subepithelial infiltrates after 2–3 weeks, superior pannus.
Tests: PCR, Giemsa (intracytoplasmic inclusions), immunofluorescence, McCoy culture.
Treat: azithromycin 1 g (repeat after a week) or doxycycline 10 days. Topical alone is not enough.
GUM clinic: other STIs, contact tracing, pregnancy test. Retest at 6–12 weeks.
Follicles and infiltrates can take months to fade.
chunks.hook: Chronic follicles in a young adult that 'won't go away' → ask about sex.

cards.q: Which C. trachomatis serovars cause adult inclusion conjunctivitis?
Treatment of choice?
cards.a: Oral azithromycin 1 g (± repeat), plus genitourinary referral.

chunks.title: Trachoma
chunks.tldr: World's leading cause of preventable blindness. Serovars A–C. Repeated infections → scarring → entropion/trichiasis → corneal opacity. WHO plan: SAFE.
points: Poverty, crowding, flies. Kids are the reservoir.
Repeated infection → type IV reaction → scarring. (Vaccines don't help: they sensitise like a first infection.)
Active (pre-school kids): follicles on the upper tarsus, papillae, superior pannus.
Cicatricial (middle age): stellate scars, Arlt line (scar band on the upper tarsus), Herbert pits (healed limbal follicles), trichiasis, entropion, dry eye, corneal opacity.
WHO grades: TF (≥5 follicles), TI (intense), TS (scarring), TT (trichiasis), CO (corneal opacity).
SAFE: Surgery (bilamellar tarsal rotation), Antibiotics (single dose azithromycin 20 mg/kg, treat the whole family/community), Face washing, Environment (water, sanitation, fly control).
chunks.hook: Herbert pits = Holes where limbal follicles used to be. Arlt line = A line of scar.

cards.q: What does SAFE stand for?
cards.a: Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement.

chunks.title: Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum)
chunks.tldr: Timing tells the bug: chemical (day 1–2) → gonococcus (week 1) → bacteria (end of week 1) → HSV (1–2 weeks) → chlamydia (1–3 weeks).
points: Conjunctivitis in the first month. Up to 10% of newborns. Usually caught during birth.
Chlamydia = commonest cause of moderate–severe cases. Can come with pneumonitis, otitis. Treat with oral erythromycin 2 weeks.
Gonococcus: hyperpurulent, very swollen lids, cornea can perforate fast. Treat with IV/IM ceftriaxone (+ cover chlamydia).
HSV (type 2): watery, lid vesicles, dendrites. Treat as systemic disease: IV aciclovir, CSF PCR for encephalitis.
Mild sticky eye: Staph, or a blocked tear duct.
Prophylaxis: povidone-iodine 2.5%, erythromycin/tetracycline ointment, silver nitrate (where gonococcus is common).
Always think of congenital glaucoma (one-sided watering!). Refer mum and partners to GUM. Notifiable.

cards.q: Neonate, day 10, mucopurulent conjunctivitis + cough. Likely organism and treatment?

chunks.title: Adenoviral conjunctivitis: the types
chunks.tldr: Adenovirus = 90% of viral conjunctivitis. Very contagious. PCF = sore throat (3, 4, 7). EKC = worst, keratitis in 80% (8, 19, 37).
points: Spread by hands, towels, instruments. Survives on surfaces for weeks. Shed before symptoms.
One eye, then the other 1–2 days later (milder). Watery, itchy/gritty, follicles, tender preauricular node.
Non-specific follicular: commonest, mild, ± cold symptoms.
Pharyngoconjunctival fever: serotypes 3, 4, 7, sore throat, family spread. Keratitis 30%.
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis: serotypes 8, 19, 37. Keratitis 80%, photophobia.
Acute haemorrhagic: enterovirus/coxsackie, tropical, big haemorrhages.
Other viruses: HSV (one-sided + skin vesicles), measles, mumps, VZV, molluscum (lid nodule).

cards.q: Adenovirus serotypes for EKC?
Follicular conjunctivitis + sore throat + fever in a child?

chunks.title: Adenovirus: cornea & treatment
chunks.tldr: Cornea: microcysts → punctate keratitis (day 7–10) → subepithelial infiltrates (immune, can last months). No antiviral works: hygiene + comfort.
points: Signs: follicles, petechial haemorrhages, chemosis, pseudomembranes (can scar).
Cornea: non-staining microcysts → staining PEK → white subepithelial infiltrates (immune response). Can recur for months or years.
Tests (if unsure): point-of-care adenovirus test (10 min), PCR. Giemsa: mononuclear cells (HSV → multinucleated giant cells).
Self-limiting in 2–3 weeks.
Infection control: hand-washing, no shared towels, clean instruments and surfaces (hypochlorite, povidone-iodine).
Comfort: cold compresses, preservative-free tears, antihistamine drops.
Steroids only for membranes or infiltrates hurting vision. They don't speed recovery, may prolong infectivity, and infiltrates rebound if stopped early. Watch the IOP.
Peel off membranes. Povidone-iodine may cut infectivity.
chunks.hook: Adeno: wash hands, wait 2–3 weeks, steroids only if you must.

cards.q: Why be cautious with steroids in adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis?
cards.a: They don't speed resolution, may prolong viral shedding, and infiltrates rebound when stopped.

chunks.title: Acute, seasonal & perennial allergic conjunctivitis
chunks.tldr: Allergy = type I (IgE, mast cells). Itch is the key symptom. Treat with dual-action drops (olopatadine, ketotifen, azelastine).
points: Acute allergic: kid playing outside → sudden dramatic chemosis + itch. Settles in hours. Cool compress ± a drop of adrenaline.
Seasonal ('hay fever eyes'): spring/summer, tree and grass pollen. Commonest form.
Perennial: all year, worse in autumn: house dust mite, pets, fungi. Milder.
Signs: red, mild papillae, chemosis, lid swelling. Vision normal. Eosinophils on scraping.
Mast cell stabilisers (cromoglicate, nedocromil, lodoxamide): take days to work, good for prevention.
Antihistamines (emedastine, epinastine, levocabastine): quick relief.
Dual-action (olopatadine, ketotifen, azelastine): fast and effective.
Rarely: NSAIDs, steroids, oral antihistamines.
chunks.hook: If it doesn't itch, it's probably not allergy.

cards.q: Allergic conjunctivitis is which hypersensitivity type?
Name a dual-action antihistamine/mast cell stabiliser drop.

chunks.title: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)
chunks.tldr: Boys from age ~5, hot dry climates, spring/summer. Cobblestone giant papillae on the upper tarsus, Trantas dots, shield ulcer. 95% grow out of it by the late teens.
points: Both IgE and cell-mediated. Mediterranean, Middle East, Africa. Most have asthma/eczema.
Symptoms: intense itch, thick ropey mucus, photophobia, lots of blinking.
Palpebral: velvety papillae → cobblestones (flat-topped) → giant papillae >1 mm with mucus between them.
Limbal (black and Asian patients): gelatinous limbal papillae + Horner–Trantas dots (white specks of eosinophils).
Cornea: superior punctate erosions → macroerosions → shield ulcer/plaque (mucus + calcium on Bowman). Shield ulcer = urgent (infection risk).
Later: grey oval subepithelial scars, pseudogerontoxon (arcus-like scar after limbal VKC), keratoconus (eye rubbing), aggressive HSV.

cards.q: White dots at the limbus in VKC?

chunks.title: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)
chunks.tldr: Adult (30–50) with lifelong eczema. Worse in winter, rarely goes away. Lower lid involved, scarring, keratoconus, shield cataract.
points: Long history of atopic dermatitis + asthma. ~5% had VKC as a child. No sex bias.
Lids: eczema (red, scaly, cracked), staph blepharitis, Hertoghe sign (outer eyebrow lost), Dennie–Morgan folds, ectropion, ptosis.
Conjunctiva: inferior more than superior (VKC is superior). Watery discharge. Smaller papillae, then scarring, symblepharon, fornix shortening, keratinised caruncle.
Cornea: inferior PEEs, vascularisation and scarring (more than VKC), persistent epithelial defects, plaques, bad HSV, bacterial/fungal infection, keratoconus (~15%).
Shield-like anterior/posterior subcapsular cataract (also from steroids).
Cataract surgery: higher endophthalmitis risk (Staph on the lids) and RD risk.
chunks.hook: VKC = Very young, goes Up (upper lid), goes away. AKC = Adult, Always there, scarring.

cards.q: Absence of the lateral eyebrows in atopic patients?
Why is endophthalmitis risk higher after cataract surgery in AKC?
cards.a: Heavy Staph aureus carriage on the lid margins.

chunks.title: Treating VKC & AKC
chunks.tldr: Base = mast cell stabiliser / dual-action drop. Flares = short, intense steroid (watch IOP). Steroid-sparing = ciclosporin or tacrolimus. Shield ulcer → debride.
points: General: avoid allergens, cool compresses, lid hygiene, moisturiser on the lid skin.
Long-term: mast cell stabiliser (cromoglicate, nedocromil, lodoxamide) ± dual-action (olopatadine, ketotifen, azelastine). NSAIDs can be added.
Flares: topical steroid (FML, loteprednol, prednisolone) 2-hourly then quick taper. Monitor IOP.
Acetylcysteine breaks up mucus and early plaques.
Ciclosporin 0.05–2%: steroid-sparing, takes weeks.
Tacrolimus ointment: lids in AKC (0.03%), and 0.1% works well for shield ulcers.
Supratarsal steroid injection for severe palpebral disease or poor compliance.
Systemic: oral antihistamine (less night rubbing), doxycycline (AKC blepharitis), immunosuppressants.
Surgery: superficial keratectomy (or PTK) for plaques/shield ulcers, amniotic membrane, glue for perforation.
chunks.hook: Stabilise daily, steroid-blitz flares, swap to ciclosporin/tacrolimus if it keeps coming back.

chunks.title: Contact lens papillary conjunctivitis (GPC) & friends
chunks.tldr: Upper tarsal papillae from rubbing on something: contact lens, prosthesis, suture, buckle, bleb. Fix = remove the trigger + new lenses.
points: CLPC: protein deposits on the lens rub the upper tarsus. Itch, mucus, blur, lens rides up (caught by the lid), can't tolerate lenses.
Papillae on the upper tarsus (giant = >1 mm, but early ones are small). Cornea is usually fine.
Other triggers: ocular prosthesis, exposed sutures, scleral buckle, filtering bleb, 'mucus fishing' (patient keeps pulling mucus out).
Treat: stop lenses for weeks, replace them, switch to daily disposables or rigid lenses (only ~5% get CLPC), preservative-free solutions, protein-removal tablets.
Drops: mast cell stabiliser (preservative-free with soft lenses), antihistamine, short steroid.
Contact allergic blepharoconjunctivitis: type IV reaction to drops, lens solutions, mascara → red, thick, scaly lid skin. Stop the cause.
Non-allergic eosinophilic conjunctivitis: middle-aged women, dry eye, eosinophils but no IgE.
chunks.hook: GPC = something keeps rubbing the upper lid. Find it and remove it.

cards.q: Which contact lens type carries the lowest risk of CLPC?
Name 3 non-CL causes of giant papillary conjunctivitis.
cards.a: Ocular prosthesis, exposed sutures, scleral buckle, filtering bleb.

chunks.title: Mucous membrane pemphigoid (OCP)
chunks.tldr: Elderly woman with chronic 'conjunctivitis' that slowly scars: shallow lower fornix → symblepharon → keratinisation. Type II, linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane. Treat systemically (dapsone first).
points: Autoimmune type II: antibodies at the basement membrane zone → blisters → scarring. Linked with HLA-DR4, DQB1. Women 2:1, old age.
Often misdiagnosed as dry eye for years.
Foster stages: I = chronic conjunctivitis + subepithelial fibrosis. II = fornix shortening (inferior). III = symblepharon. IV = keratinisation + ankyloblepharon.
Lids: trichiasis, keratinised lid margin, ankyloblepharon (lids stuck together at the outer canthus).
Cornea: epithelial defects, vessels, stem cell failure → conjunctivalisation, opacity.
Body: mouth blisters (common), oesophageal/laryngeal strictures, skin blisters (25%).
Biopsy: linear antibody + complement at the BMZ.
Treat systemically: dapsone (check G6PD first!) → azathioprine/methotrexate/MMF → cyclophosphamide, steroids for rapid control, IVIG, rituximab.
Local: preservative-free tears, lid care, retinoic acid. Surgery only when quiet: avoid cutting conjunctiva, mucous membrane grafts, keratoprosthesis at the end.
chunks.hook: Measure the lower fornix in any old person with chronic red eyes. Dapsone → check G6PD.

cards.q: Foster stage III OCP?
Test before starting dapsone?
Immunofluorescence finding in MMP?
cards.a: Linear IgG/IgA/C3 deposition at the basement membrane zone.

chunks.title: Stevens–Johnson / TEN
chunks.tldr: Drug reaction (sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, nevirapine…) → flu-like illness → mouth and lip crusting + skin sloughing. Eye: membranes acutely, scarring later. Check the eyes daily.
points: Type IV, usually a drug: sulfonamides, trimethoprim, paracetamol, nevirapine, anticonvulsants. Also Mycoplasma, HSV.
TEN = severe form. SJS mortality ~5% (TEN much higher). Young adults.
Flu-like up to 2 weeks → haemorrhagic crusting of lips, mouth/genital blisters, purpuric/necrotic skin. (Target lesions = erythema multiforme, a different disease.)
Acute eye: haemorrhagic lid crusts, conjunctivitis, membranes/pseudomembranes, epithelial defects, iritis.
Late eye: symblepharon, keratinised lid margin/conjunctiva, trichiasis, entropion, dry eye, corneal vessels and scarring.
Systemic: stop the drug, fluids/nutrition, burns unit. Steroids/IVIG are controversial.
Acute eye care: daily review, preservative-free lubricants hourly, break early symblephara with a glass rod, scleral ring, topical steroid, cycloplegic, consider amniotic membrane.
Chronic: lubricate, plugs, retinoic acid, scleral lenses, mucous membrane grafts, limbal stem cells, keratoprosthesis.
Ocular GVHD (after stem-cell transplant, 40–60%): looks like SJS: dry eye, membranes, scarring. Main treatment: topical ciclosporin.
chunks.hook: New drug + crusty bleeding lips + red eyes = SJS. Sweep the fornices daily.

cards.q: Drug classes most often triggering SJS?
Acute measure to prevent symblepharon in SJS?
cards.a: Daily lysis with a glass rod, scleral ring, (amniotic membrane).

chunks.title: SLK, ligneous, Parinaud, factitious
chunks.tldr: SLK → check the thyroid. Ligneous → plasminogen deficiency, woody membranes. Parinaud oculoglandular → cat scratch. Factitious → inferior staining only.
points: Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis: middle-aged women, ~50% thyroid disease. Red radial band of superior bulbar conjunctiva, limbal papillae, velvety upper tarsus, superior PEEs, filaments. Symptoms > signs.
SLK cause: loose superior conjunctiva rubbed by blinking. Treat: lubricants, acetylcysteine, ciclosporin, bandage CL, silver nitrate 0.5%, resect superior conjunctiva.

Ligneous conjunctivitis: kids (~5 y), woody fibrin pseudomembranes on the tarsus. Plasminogen deficiency. Can affect gums, lungs, kidneys. Stop antifibrinolytics. Excise + topical heparin + steroid, topical plasminogen.
Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome: fever + one-sided granulomatous conjunctivitis + big preauricular node. Bartonella henselae (cat scratch). Also tularaemia, TB, syphilis, sporotrichosis.
Factitious: self-inflicted. Inferior injection/staining with a quiet superior conjunctiva, linear abrasions, Candida. Avoid confrontation, consider psychiatry.

chunks.title: Pinguecula & pterygium
chunks.tldr: Both are UV damage. Pinguecula stays off the cornea. Pterygium grows onto the cornea. Pterygium surgery: conjunctival autograft (or MMC) to stop recurrence.
points: Pinguecula: yellow-white bump next to the limbus (nasal more often). Harmless. Can get inflamed (pingueculitis) → lubricant or short steroid.
Pterygium: triangle of fibrovascular tissue over the limbus, invading Bowman layer. Parts: cap, head, body.
Signs: Stocker line (iron line in front of the head), Fuchs islets (flecks at the edge).
Problems: irritation (dellen), astigmatism, blocks the visual axis, cosmetic, restricted movement if recurrent.
Pseudopterygium: after a burn, ulcer or trauma. Off the horizontal, only stuck at the apex (a probe passes under it).
Surgery: bare sclera alone → ~80% recurrence. Conjunctival autograft (sutured or fibrin glue) or mitomycin C / beta radiation lowers recurrence. Wear sunglasses.
chunks.hook: Pinguecula = Parked (stays off the cornea). Pterygium = Pushes in.

cards.q: Iron line in the epithelium ahead of a pterygium?
Recurrence rate after bare-sclera excision?
How to tell a pseudopterygium?
cards.a: Off the horizontal, adherent only at its apex (probe passes under), history of injury/ulcer.

chunks.title: Little stuff: concretions, cysts, subconj haemorrhage
chunks.tldr: Concretions = yellow specks on the lower tarsus (pick out if they scratch). Subconjunctival haemorrhage = scary-looking but usually harmless: check BP; in a baby think abuse or scurvy.
points: Concretions: tiny yellow-white keratin deposits, inferior tarsus/fornix. Age, trachoma. Remove with a needle if eroding through.
Conjunctivochalasis: loose lower fold → watering, irritation. Lubricate, treat blepharitis, resect if severe.
Retention cyst: clear bubble on the bulbar conjunctiva. Puncture (recurs) → excise.
Lymphangiectasia: string of sausage-shaped clear channels, can fill with blood.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage: often spontaneous, coughing/sneezing, contact lenses (young), hypertension, aspirin/anticoagulants. Clears in 1–2 weeks.
Infant with subconj haemorrhage → consider non-accidental injury and vitamin C deficiency.
chunks.hook: Old person bleed → check BP. Baby bleed → think abuse.
